title: Confusion Counts by Model and Condition
note: A document counts as a true positive only if every annotated gap is found and no unsupported gap is reported. TN are the 30 gap-free control documents left correctly untouched.

title: Evaluation Metrics by Model and Condition
note: Balanced score is the unweighted mean of recall over gapped documents and specificity over controls. A strategy that never reports anything scores 0.500, so gap-level columns are reported alongside.

title: Documents Solved out of 150
note: Completely correct documents, gapped and control combined.

title: Exact McNemar Tests, Paired on Documents
note: Exact binomial rather than chi-square, because discordant counts are single-digit. 3 of 15 comparisons reach p < .05, and all of them involve condition C.
footnote: No A-vs-B comparison is significant in any model; the smallest is p = .058 for GPT-5.6-terra.

title: Documents Solved by Complexity Tier
note: C0 = 30 docs / 30 gaps, C1 = 30/30, C2 = 30/60, C3 = 38/138, Zero-Gaps = 22 controls. Tiers vary both the number of gaps per document and their subtlety, and these do not increase together.

title: Gap-Level Diagnostics
note: Secondary diagnostic. Gap-level recall credits partial recovery that the all-or-nothing document rule discards.

title: Failure Modes among False-Negative Documents
note: Why a gapped document failed. 'Complete but unsupported' means every annotated gap was found but an extra gap was also reported, which the scoring rule charges as a full failure.

title: Total Spend and Reliability
note: Actual billed amounts from the project's Bedrock call log, computed from returned token counts. Claude Sonnet 5 was the only model to fail at all; those failures predate the max_tokens fix.

title: Cost-Effectiveness at Each Model's Best Condition
note: Dollars per completely solved document and per annotated gap recovered, at whichever condition each model performed best.
footnote: GPT-5.6-terra solves the most documents at one third the cost of Claude Sonnet 5, with zero failures.

title: Per-Call Economics, Condition B
note: Successful calls only. Averaging over failed calls would understate the real cost of a usable prediction.
footnote: Sonnet 5's input is roughly 1.9x the others for an identical prompt: its tokenizer is less efficient on this text.

title: Extended Reasoning: Cost and Effect
note: Claude Sonnet 5 on condition C, run twice with identical inputs. Disabling reasoning cut output by 87% and cost by 39% — and made the model unusable.
footnote: Balanced document score fell from 0.617 to 0.275 with reasoning disabled (exact McNemar p < .0001, 49 documents broken against 3 fixed).

title: Failure Rate by Model
note: Bedrock's default 4,096-token output cap was silently in force until max_tokens was forwarded explicitly. Reasoning-heavy generations exhausted the budget before emitting an answer.

title: Cost of Conditions A + B against Pooled Gap Recall
source: benchmark_v2 · 300 calls per model · Bedrock call log
note: Pooled across conditions A (raw text) and B (raw text + induced schema), 150 documents each. Cost is billed spend for those 300 calls.
footnote: GPT-5.6-terra finds more gaps than Claude Sonnet 5 for roughly a quarter of the spend. Devstral-123B costs more than either open model while finding the fewest gaps.

title: Referential Integrity Checks
note: All four checks are enforced at generation time against identifiers in the current schema, so this falsifies a failure of that constraint rather than establishing schema quality independently.

title: Provenance Coverage
note: Section-level coverage is complete. Document-level traceability is weaker: none of the 189 provenance records names the document its section pointer indexes.

title: Near-Duplicate Concept Pairs, Ranked and Adjudicated
note: Eight of the eighteen pairs at similarity 0.80 or above were manually adjudicated by one author. The three confirmed duplicates scored 0.807-0.828, below all four pairs judged correctly distinct.

title: Detection Rate by Perturbation Type
note: Share of the 15 runs (5 models × 3 conditions) that found each gap, grouped by how the gap was injected. Overall rate 0.527. ADD added carve-out · THR threshold qualifier · REM removal · ACT actor swap · OMI omission · SCP scope · CON condition · EXI existing-duty edit · MOD modality · NEG negation
footnote: The 15 runs per gap are not independent — they read the same sentence — so the z-tests are over-confident. Use them to rank, not to infer.

title: Detection Rate by Reference Section
note: Standardised holds every section to the corpus-wide perturbation mix, so topic and perturbation type are separated. The spread narrows only from 0.214 to 0.191, so about 89% of the topic effect is not explained by the mix.

title: Detection Rate by Topic
note: Topics are the reference Code of Conduct's own bullet labels. Where the document gives a bullet no label, its opening words are quoted instead. Anti-corruption and audit topics occupy every position at the hard end.
rows: Expression of opinion, personal rights, and privacy
Conflict minerals and high-risk raw materials
footnote: Rows backed by fewer than about 30 gold gaps move by whole gaps; read the ranking rather than the individual values.

title: Perturbation Type by Model
note: Conditions pooled. Threshold edits are the one type that defeats the frontier models too: GPT-5.6-terra scores 0.90 or above on every other well-sampled row and 0.701 here. Qwen3-235B never detects an omission in 126 attempts.
footnote: ADD, REM, ACT and CON have 3–9 gaps corpus-wide, so their per-model cells rest on 9–27 attempts. THR, OMI, SCP, MOD and EXI are the reliable rows.

title: Reference Section by Model
note: Conditions pooled. The topic effect is far larger in the weak models (spread 0.45 for gpt-oss-120B) than the strong ones (0.18 for GPT-5.6-terra), but it does not vanish: Business integrity and Verification are the weakest sections for all five models.

title: Perturbation Type by Condition
note: Models pooled. The schema does not rescue any gap type. Threshold edits, the hardest type, get worse under BT (0.313 to 0.246); the only positive moves are on types with three to six gaps.

title: Reference Section by Condition
note: Models pooled. Adding the schema is flat or slightly negative in every section. There is no topic where the schema recovers the aggregate null.

title: Topic by Condition
note: Models pooled. Across the 36 topics the schema is better by more than 0.05 in four and worse in eleven. A paired sign test at the gap-by-model level, Holm-corrected over all 36 topics, finds no topic where BT differs from A: the smallest raw p is 0.180.
rows: Expression of opinion, personal rights, and privacy
Conflict minerals and high-risk raw materials
footnote: Pooled over every topic, BT fixed 93 gaps and broke 121 (sign test p = 0.065). The visible per-topic swings are noise on three to six gaps.

note: Four of the 258 gaps were missed by all five models in all three conditions. Every one is a threshold edit: a single qualifying adverb inserted into a categorical duty, which changes the legal force while leaving the sentence almost unchanged.
